title_en: Apple is set to show off new smart home devices at an October 13 event
title_fa: Apple is set to show off new smart home devices at an October 13 event
excerpt_en: The event is set for 9AM ET.
excerpt_fa: The event is set for 9AM ET.
content_en:
Apple is set to show off new smart home devices at an October 13 event
The event, which it teased with the tagline "Welcome home," is set for 9AM ET.
Apple has announced its second event of the fall, and it sure seems like this one will be focused on smart home products. The event, which it's teased with the phrase, "Welcome home," is set for October 13 at 9AM ET. "We look forward to welcoming you to an Apple Experience," the company said in an invite. The event will take place in Tribeca, New York.
It had been expected for a while that the company would hold an event on that date. Along with refreshed versions of the Apple TV and HomePod mini, it's said that Apple will unveil its long-expected HomePad.
Welcome home. October 13. pic.twitter.com/ChelGSDOTI
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 8, 2026
It's been rumored for years that Apple has been working on a smart display to rival the likes of Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Next Hub. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported that Apple delayed the device until Siri AI was ready.
The HomePad (as it's expected to be called) is said to have a seven-inch display, a fresh operating system dubbed homeOS and a dashboard that looks similar to the StandBy mode on iPhones. Rumors suggest it'll use face and voice recognition to personalize content based on the person who's operating it at the time. Along with the ability to control smart home products, it's believed that the HomePad will support FaceTime calls, video and music streaming, intercom communication with other devices and many other features.
As for the new Apple TV and HomePod mini, it's likely that those are getting spec upgrades so they can support Siri AI. However, recent macOS beta code suggests the revamped speaker may also gain a display with an Apple Watch-style interface.
October is shaping up to be a big month for Apple. Not only does the company have this latest event on deck, it's set to release the iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, in a couple of weeks.

title_en: Natura’s $99 smart ring puts AI agents on your finger
title_fa: Natura’s $99 smart ring puts AI agents on your finger
excerpt_en: Natura’s $99 Interface smart ring lets you summon AI agents with the press of a finger to complete tasks, capture thoughts, and control devices — while doubling as a health tracker.
excerpt_fa: Natura’s $99 Interface smart ring lets you summon AI agents with the press of a finger to complete tasks, capture thoughts, and control devices — while doubling as a health tracker.
content_en:
Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity.
The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square. After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person.
The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more.
Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January.
The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology.
“Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.”
The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker.
Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app.
Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else.
In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent.
“Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.”
Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price. For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so. After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans to charge a $9 monthly subscription fee.
The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components. However, Natura plans to price its ring lower initially to reduce the barrier to entry and drive adoption.
As for health tracking, the ring tracks heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, different sleep stages, daily movement and step count, and skin temperature over time.
The company says the ring can last six to 12 days on a full charge, depending on usage, and takes 100 minutes to fully recharge.
While the smart ring market is filled with health-focused offerings from companies like Oura, Ultrahuman, and RingConn, as well as AI-focused ones from companies like Pebble and Vocci, Ferraris believes Interface stands out by combining both worlds.
“This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small. The product itself is, from a hardware perspective, very different from anything else that’s out there.”

title_en: Goodfire says its new ‘inside-out’ monitors catch rogue AI agents at a fraction of the cost
title_fa: Goodfire says its new ‘inside-out’ monitors catch rogue AI agents at a fraction of the cost
excerpt_en: Goodfire just launched what it says is a cheaper way to keep AI agents in check: Instead of paying a second AI to read everything an agent does, its monitors peek inside the model while it works and only call in backup when something looks fishy.
excerpt_fa: Goodfire just launched what it says is a cheaper way to keep AI agents in check: Instead of paying a second AI to read everything an agent does, its monitors peek inside the model while it works and only call in backup when something looks fishy.
content_en:
The standard way to keep an AI agent in line is to have a second AI read over its shoulder. It’s been the default approach, but it can get expensive fast when agents run for hours and process the equivalent of several novels’ worth of text.
Goodfire, a startup focused on interpretability (figuring out how AI models work internally), launched a cheaper option on Thursday: monitors that watch what’s happening inside an AI model as it works, rather than just reading what it writes. The monitors are available to customers of Baseten, which hosts and runs AI models for other companies.
Baseten’s Base Labs announced a safety partnership with Goodfire and the AI platform Hugging Face last month.
The launch comes after a string of incidents this year in which AI agents escaped their test environments, including OpenAI agents that breached Hugging Face. Kimi K3, the open model Goodfire built its first monitor around, took advantage of a leak in its sandbox to access the internet and information on GitHub this summer.
Goodfire’s system works a bit like airport security. Small detectors called probes read the model’s internal signals at every step of an agent’s work, the way a walk-through scanner checks every passenger. Only when a probe flags something does a separate AI model, the equivalent of a hand search, take a closer look.
Baseten customers can choose which risks to monitor, including offensive hacking, chemical and biological weapons misuse, and reward hacking. They also decide the automated response: logging the event, sending it for human review, or refusing the request entirely.
Goodfire says its approach is also cheaper to run. Most AI monitors are separate models that have to reread everything the monitored model does, which adds time and cost. Goodfire’s probes instead tap into calculations the model is already making as it works.
“Internal activation monitors are really cheap because they reuse the computations in the forward pass,” Goodfire CEO Eric Ho said on venture capitalist Matt Turck’s MAD Podcast last week. “So the model’s already computing this token. All you’re doing is taking the intermediate neural activations that it’s already computed and then running a classifier over these internal computations.” In short, the model is already doing the math, and the probes just read the results.
In Goodfire’s tests on Kimi K3, monitoring about 1 million exchanges would cost roughly $185, compared with $5420 for a cheaper AI model checking every step and about $200,000 for a top-tier one. The probes caught 93% of malicious hacking sessions and sent 5.5% of harmless ones for a second look
Running four probes at once added less than 2% to the time it takes the model to start responding, the company said.
“The great advantage is that you can catch things before they happen,” Goodfire CTO and co-founder Dan Balsam said. “We can detect when the model might hack during eval or training.”
The pitch is aimed at open models. Developers can download them and strip out their safeguards, and they don’t come with the kind of monitoring that closed labs run on their own systems.
“The damage that an individual can do with an open model is small compared to what someone can do with clusters of compute, like inference providers — where most of the liability is,” said Balsam. “When we have the open ‘Mythos’ moment, it’s going to become clear that models need guardrails deployed at inference time.”
Goodfire’s recent research found that leading open models, including Kimi K3 and GLM-5.2, reward-hacked in 50% to 96% of runs on tests of AI agents.
Goodfire isn’t the first to try this approach. Google DeepMind said in January that its research informed the deployment of misuse-detection probes in Gemini.
Balsam said the monitors are the near-term piece of a longer research goal: reverse-engineering an LLM so that behavior can be traced back to where it emerged in training. “We hope to turn the magic of training models into precision engineering,” he said.

title_en: US bars Microsoft, Adobe, and major IT firms from green card program for skilled foreign workers
title_fa: US bars Microsoft, Adobe, and major IT firms from green card program for skilled foreign workers
excerpt_en: The other firms being suspended from the program include Capgemini, Cognizant, HCL, Infosys, Tata, and Wipro.
excerpt_fa: The other firms being suspended from the program include Capgemini, Cognizant, HCL, Infosys, Tata, and Wipro.
content_en:
The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft, Adobe, and several other technology companies from a program that helps skilled foreign workers obtain permanent residency in the United States, accusing the companies of fraud.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” U.S. Vice President JD Vance said in a news conference on Thursday, Reuters reported.
The other firms being suspended from the program include Capgemini, Cognizant, HCL, Infosys, Tata, and Wipro. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said the government would not accept any new or pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies.
H-1B visas are designed for highly skilled positions that employers may struggle to fill with qualified U.S. workers. Tech companies are among the largest users of the program, with nearly three-quarters of approved visas going to workers from India, according to The Associated Press.
“We believe in the strength and talent of the American workforce,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans. We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information. For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
The statement continues, “These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.”
The company went on to note that it only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the “rigorous standards” of the visa category, and that pays its H-1B employees the same as any “other employees doing comparable work.”
Vance also said during the news conference that the administration would investigate nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, and Stanford, over allegations they’re abusing a program that allows international students to come to the U.S. and were using the program to undermine wages for American workers.
Adobe did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Update 10/08/2026 1:50pm ET: The article was updated to include a statement from Microsoft.

title_en: Careful out there: latest GTA 6 leak has major story spoilers
title_fa: Careful out there: latest GTA 6 leak has major story spoilers
excerpt_en: If you can't help yourself, maybe don't watch it at work...
excerpt_fa: If you can't help yourself, maybe don't watch it at work...
content_en:
Careful out there: latest GTA 6 leak has major story spoilers
A lengthy video also shows one of the protagonists fully nude.
The Grand Theft Auto VI leaks keep coming and this latest one is the biggest of all, according to a report by Kotaku. Cyberleek, the unknown person or group behind all of this footage, has dropped a 25-minute video of the game in action. It's making the rounds and will likely soon be all over social media.
It's riddled with story spoilers (and ads for the leaker's memecoin) so that's a strong reason to avoid watching it if you want to go into the game cold on November 19. Be extra vigilant while perusing social media for the next few days.
I watched the footage and there is one spoiler I'm willing to discuss. The video shows co-protagonist Jason fully nude. Yeah. He hangs dong. As a matter of fact, it seems to suggest that the game is fully playable with Jason in the raw.
That's pretty wild, but it's also highly plausible that all of Cyberleek's footage is from an earlier build of the game. We don't actually know what Rockstar has in store for us, though the company's legal team has been busy playing whack-a-mole with leaked clips. I fully expect its lawyers to go into hyperdrive now that story spoilers are out there.
As previously mentioned, GTA 6 finally comes out on November 19. That's just over a month away. It's been over 13 years since GTA 5 hit store shelves. Speaking of store shelves, physical copies of the game will not include actual discs. It's one of those "code in a box" type things.

title_en: New York alleges TikTok gave teens, children a placebo safety feature instead of a real one
title_fa: New York alleges TikTok gave teens, children a placebo safety feature instead of a real one
excerpt_en: New York’s lawsuit against the company is one of more than two dozen cases brought by states accusing the social media giant of designing its platform to encourage addictive use among children.
excerpt_fa: New York’s lawsuit against the company is one of more than two dozen cases brought by states accusing the social media giant of designing its platform to encourage addictive use among children.
content_en:
TikTok gave teens and children access to a placebo safety feature instead of a real one that would have let them refresh their recommendations in an experiment, according to allegations in New York’s lawsuit against the social media platform.
Reuters reports that TikTok’s experiments involved thousands of users, including teens and children, who had opted to use safety features like “Algo Refresh,” a tool that allows users to reset their recommendations and stop seeing unwanted or potentially harmful content.
Although the users believed that they had activated the feature, their feeds didn’t change, unlike those of users who weren’t part of the experiment and had access to a fully functioning version of the tool.
New York’s lawsuit against the company is one of more than two dozen cases brought by states that accuse the social media giant of designing its platform to encourage addictive use among children and misleading users about its safety.
“We continuously make improvements to our platform which means that, like most companies, we regularly test new products and features to validate the experience and understand how they work in the real world,” TikTok told told Reuters.
TikTok did not immediately return a request for comment.
The lawsuit also claims that TikTok conducted other experiments. Bloomberg reported in June that one such experiment withheld a safety feature from 15 million U.S. users, including a teenager who later died by suicide.

title_en: Asos confirms breach of customer data after hackers send rogue app notification
title_fa: Asos confirms breach of customer data after hackers send rogue app notification
excerpt_en: The hackers alerted the fashion giant's customers through a push notification that said they had "fully compromised" the company's cloud storage.
excerpt_fa: The hackers alerted the fashion giant's customers through a push notification that said they had "fully compromised" the company's cloud storage.
content_en:
U.K. fashion retail giant Asos has confirmed a data breach of its customers’ personal information after hackers used the company’s own app to notify users that the company had been compromised.
Asos said in a filing with the London Stock Exchange that hackers broke into a third-party platform hosting data that the company uses to communicate with customers.
The company said that names and contact information were taken in the breach.
BBC News reports that the stolen data includes home addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses, as well as notes relating to customer profiles, such as their website search queries.
Asos said the hackers sent an “unauthorised customer notification,” which many posted to social media. The notification addressed Asos’ data protection officer and IT department and said that the hackers “fully compromised” the company’s data hosted on Snowflake, a tech company that allows its corporate customers to analyze large amounts of data. “Engage with us, or we will leak it,” the notification reads.
By using the app’s own notification system to alert customers, the hackers are trying to pressure the company into engaging with them or risk having the stolen data published online.
The hackers reportedly broke into the Snowflake instance by “impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials,” reports Bleeping Computer. Snowflake said it had not experienced a breach of its systems. It’s unclear if the Asos-run Snowflake instance was protected with multi-factor authentication. It’s also not known how the hackers gained access to Asos’ system for sending in-app push notifications, which is often handled by a third-party service.
The hackers, who go by the handle Xuanye Group, have not indicated how much data they allegedly possess. Asos has 17 million customers, according to its website.
Earlier this year, fintech giant Betterment was compromised by hackers who used their access to the company’s third-party marketing platform to impersonate the company and send a crypto scam to its customers. The hackers also accessed customer names, email addresses, and phone numbers, among other data, during the breach.

excerpt_fa: Ambrosia Energy CEO Ben Longmier and Bloom Energy SVP Bill Thayer join the Smart Systems Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt. Register now to save up to $100. Grab a second of the same pass to save 50%.
content_en:
AI may be built in software, but scaling it is becoming a physical-world problem. Every new model, agent, and AI application needs somewhere to run, and an infrastructure connecting them all.
At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Ben Longmier, CEO of Ambrosia Energy, and Bill Thayer, SVP and Head of Datacenter Solutions at Bloom Energy, come together on the Smart Systems Stage for a conversation on “Where the AI Infrastructure Boom Is Creating Winners.”
This industry stage session will examine which constraints are creating durable business opportunities, where new categories are beginning to emerge, and what founders can build as AI moves further into the physical world.
Get your pass now to save up to $100 before rates go up at the door on October 13. Grab a second pass at 50% off. Register now.
The AI race is becoming an infrastructure race
Much of the AI conversation has focused on models, chips, and applications. But none of them operate in isolation. Scaling AI depends on an expanding physical stack: power generation, grid connections, data centers, cooling, electrical equipment, and the systems required to keep everything running.
That creates a different kind of challenge. What happens when demand for compute grows faster than power and infrastructure can be delivered? Which shortages are temporary, and which could reshape the market for years? Where does a constraint stop being a problem and start becoming a category of its own? Those are the questions this session will tackle.
Rather than looking at AI solely through the software layer, Bill Thayer and Ben Longmier will examine the infrastructure underneath it — and what those pressures could mean for founders, investors, and companies planning for the next phase of AI growth.
Where do the real opportunities sit?
Infrastructure booms create opportunity, but the benefits are rarely distributed evenly. The challenge is identifying which parts of the stack genuinely need new solutions, where spending is likely to persist, and which emerging categories can support durable businesses rather than short-term demand.
Bringing together leaders across energy, data center solutions, and market intelligence gives the discussion a wider view of that question. Expect the conversation to explore where constraints are appearing, how the market is responding, and which areas founders should be watching as more capital flows into AI infrastructure.
For founders, that means looking beyond the obvious AI application. For investors, it means understanding where infrastructure demand could create defensible markets. For tech leaders, it offers a clearer view of the physical systems increasingly shaping where and how AI can scale.
The next AI company may solve a physical-world problem
The next major opportunity created by AI may not look like an AI company at all. It could emerge in energy, data centers, cooling, grid technology, electrical equipment, infrastructure software, or entirely new categories that don’t yet have established names.
The common factor is the same: AI is creating new demands on the physical world, and those demands need solutions. That is what makes this session broader than an infrastructure discussion. It’s about understanding where the next markets could emerge — and who is positioned to build for them.
Join Ben Longmier and Bill Thayer at the Smart Systems Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and explore where the AI infrastructure boom is creating its next opportunities. Don’t forget about the 250+ speakers leading 200+ sessions.
Save up to $100 before doors open at Moscone West on October 13 at 8 a.m. PT. Bring a co-founder, partner, colleague, or peer and get 50% off a second pass of the same ticket type.

title_en: Spotify is getting more serious about selling enterprise software
title_fa: Spotify is getting more serious about selling enterprise software
excerpt_en: The company launched technology.spotify.com, a new site that will make its internal tech available to outsiders.
excerpt_fa: The company launched technology.spotify.com, a new site that will make its internal tech available to outsiders.
content_en:
Spotify is formalizing efforts around its enterprise and developer tools business with Thursday’s launch of technology.spotify.com, a new site that will make its internal tech available to outsiders.
The company’s foray into this space is not exactly new. As Spotify points out in its announcement of the new site, it’s been offering different products to the wider tech community since 2020 when it open sourced Backstage, a platform and framework for building customizable developer portals.
It has also been selling its enterprise-focused software experimentation platform Confidence since 2023 and its enterprise software development platform Portal since 2024. Earlier this year, it began selling its developer tool for managing AI coding agents, Xirp.
While many technology companies build their own internal systems to help their developers work more efficiently, it’s somewhat unusual to see a company like Spotify sell those tools to other businesses.
Spotify’s SVP of Technology & Platform, Tyson Singer, acknowledged that the company’s move into this space has raised questions.
“I get asked a version of this question every day: why is Spotify in the business of selling software?,” he wrote in a post on Spotify’s engineering site. “The truth is, the Spotify you know and love is more than a great streaming service. Behind our consumer app are hundreds of cross-functional squads shipping products and code day in, day out,” he explained.
The new technology website will house the solutions Spotify has built to serve its own audience of 777 million monthly active users, including both open source and paid services.
Though AI has made building such software faster, Spotify points out that this doesn’t necessarily mean it’s simpler — “the complexity, the cost and the operational surface area all grow with it,” Singer wrote. The company’s bet is that, despite AI’s advances, software development teams will still require certain core services, like those Spotify sells, which it says will be agent-ready.
So far, it’s unclear how much revenue Spotify’s enterprise sales are generating, as the company hasn’t disclosed those figures in its financial reporting. That could potentially change as Spotify makes a more concerted push into the enterprise market, turning what was once a side business into a more formal operation.
The technology website doesn’t include pricing; instead, companies can fill out a form to contact sales and discuss their needs.
content_fa:
Spotify is formalizing efforts around its enterprise and developer tools business with Thursday’s launch of technology.spotify.com, a new site that will make its internal tech available to outsiders.
The company’s foray into this space is not exactly new. As Spotify points out in its announcement of the new site, it’s been offering different products to the wider tech community since 2020 when it open sourced Backstage, a platform and framework for building customizable developer portals.
It has also been selling its enterprise-focused software experimentation platform Confidence since 2023 and its enterprise software development platform Portal since 2024. Earlier this year, it began selling its developer tool for managing AI coding agents, Xirp.
While many technology companies build their own internal systems to help their developers work more efficiently, it’s somewhat unusual to see a company like Spotify sell those tools to other businesses.
Spotify’s SVP of Technology & Platform, Tyson Singer, acknowledged that the company’s move into this space has raised questions.
“I get asked a version of this question every day: why is Spotify in the business of selling software?,” he wrote in a post on Spotify’s engineering site. “The truth is, the Spotify you know and love is more than a great streaming service. Behind our consumer app are hundreds of cross-functional squads shipping products and code day in, day out,” he explained.
The new technology website will house the solutions Spotify has built to serve its own audience of 777 million monthly active users, including both open source and paid services.
Though AI has made building such software faster, Spotify points out that this doesn’t necessarily mean it’s simpler — “the complexity, the cost and the operational surface area all grow with it,” Singer wrote. The company’s bet is that, despite AI’s advances, software development teams will still require certain core services, like those Spotify sells, which it says will be agent-ready.
So far, it’s unclear how much revenue Spotify’s enterprise sales are generating, as the company hasn’t disclosed those figures in its financial reporting. That could potentially change as Spotify makes a more concerted push into the enterprise market, turning what was once a side business into a more formal operation.
The technology website doesn’t include pricing; instead, companies can fill out a form to contact sales and discuss their needs.

title_en: Xbox's new division will focus on TV and movie adaptations of its biggest franchises
title_fa: Xbox's new division will focus on TV and movie adaptations of its biggest franchises
excerpt_en: No really, how are you going to adapt Candy Crush.
excerpt_fa: No really, how are you going to adapt Candy Crush.
content_en:
Xbox's new division will focus on TV and movie adaptations of its biggest franchises
Products and events will also be part of XP’s strategy.
A new division of Xbox called XP will focus on growing the fanbases of its various gaming properties through TV, film, products and events. Announced in a blog post written by Xbox's Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball, XP will seemingly play a significant role in the company's plan to become "the number one entertainment company in the world," and one that has set the lofty ambition of entertaining one billion people each and every day.
Microsoft hasn't paired this news with the announcement of any new movies or globetrotting concerts, but we do have a pretty good idea of how the new games-adjacent division will function. XP will be tasked with bringing Xbox's "worlds and characters to new audiences through film, television, and other forms of linear storytelling," as well as appealing to the existing Xbox community through "authentic" product launches, live events and attractions. The division will also seek to forge partnerships with creators and brands.
XP will be headed up by Kayleen Walters, who worked at Lucasfilm for 13 years before joining Microsoft and eventually becoming president of Minecraft studio Mojang. Walters also served as an executive producer on last year's box office-smashing (and notably not terrible) A Minecraft Movie, and is named as a producer on the upcoming sequel. A Minecraft theme park is set to open its doors in the UK next year, the promotion of which presumably now also falls within XP's remit.
Microsoft doubling down on its transmedia strategy isn't surprising when you consider its vast library of IP. The live-action Halo show may not have turned out as well as it would have liked, but Prime Video's Fallout has been a pretty big success, while an eventual Call of Duty movie was surely inevitable as soon as the ink was dry on the company's Activision acquisition.
According to The Hollywood Reporter, there are additional plans to adapt the likes of Gears of War, Candy Crush, Diablo, Forza and The Elder Scrolls in the future. Xbox also said it intends to collaborate with Kojima Productions on TV and film projects after swooping in to claim publishing rights for the Metal Gear Solid creator's upcoming action-espionage game, Physint, after Sony surprisingly let it go.

title_en: Waymo locks in $5B loan from Blackstone, PIMCO to fuel robotaxi expansion
title_fa: Waymo locks in $5B loan from Blackstone, PIMCO to fuel robotaxi expansion
excerpt_en: This is the first time the Alphabet-owned company has turned to debt financing.
excerpt_fa: This is the first time the Alphabet-owned company has turned to debt financing.
content_en:
Waymo, the autonomous vehicle technology company under Google parent Alphabet, closed a $5 billion loan from a series of high-profile lenders, including PIMCO, Blackstone, and Sixth Street.
The debt financing — Waymo’s first — comes as the company accelerates its commercial expansion within existing cities while pushing into new markets in the United States, Europe, and Japan. Waymo described the debt financing as an important step in its evolution into a “scaling commercial enterprise.”
Other lenders in the $5 billion loan include Capital Group, Loomis Sayles, T. Rowe Price, Apollo, Blue Owl, Diameter Capital Partners, Franklin Templeton, Fidelity Management & Research Company, HPS Investment Partners, and Oaktree, Waymo said on Thursday. Goldman Sachs served as the sole lead bookrunner.
Until now, Waymo has relied on capital from its parent company and outside investors. In February, Waymo raised $16 billion in equity from investors that pushed its valuation to $126 billion. Dragoneer Investment Group, DST Global, and Sequoia Capital led the funding round. Alphabet, which supported the round, has maintained its position as majority investor. The company raised $5.6 billion in a Series C funding round in 2024, $2.5 billion in 2021, and $3.2 billion in 2020.
A Waymo spokesperson said in an email that the debt financing will give the company financial flexibility to strengthen its balance sheet and position it to “capitalize on the significant opportunities ahead, especially as a scaling business with proven commercial demand and improved road safety outcomes in the communities in which we operate.”
Formerly a self-driving project within Google, Waymo spent years testing its autonomous vehicle tech on public roads in Silicon Valley and the Bay Area and providing the occasional public or media demo. The company expanded in 2016 to Phoenix, which would become its first robotaxi market.
In August 2023, Waymo received the final necessary permit to operate a robotaxi service and charge for rides in California, a milestone that would kick off a more aggressive commercial playbook. Since then, Waymo has launched in multiple California cities, including Los Angeles, San Francisco, and, more recently San Diego. It has also brought its robotaxi service to numerous other U.S. markets, including Austin, Dallas, and Houston in Texas and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. Waymo now offers robotaxi services in 15 markets.
Waymo is keen to take its robotaxi services global, too. The company is testing in London and Tokyo and plans to launch in those cities.
The company’s growth has also spurred criticism and increased attention from regulators.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation opened an investigation into the illegal behavior of Waymo robotaxis around school buses. The federal safety regulator also launched an investigation after a Waymo robotaxi hit a child near a school. The child, who sustained minor injuries, was struck at about six mph. Earlier this year, the National Transportation Safety Board opened its own investigation into Waymo after its robotaxis were spotted illegally passing stopped school buses numerous times in at least two states.

title_en: The new Stylophone Mini packs in iconic sounds and comes in three nifty colors
title_fa: The new Stylophone Mini packs in iconic sounds and comes in three nifty colors
excerpt_en: It's little because it's small, and it's small because it's little.
excerpt_fa: It's little because it's small, and it's small because it's little.
content_en:
The new Stylophone Mini packs in iconic sounds and comes in three nifty colors
It's small enough to attach to a keychain and costs just $30.
The quirky Stylophone synthesizer has been around since the 1960s. You've probably heard it on tracks like David Bowie's "Space Oddity." As a matter of fact, he wrote much of the song on one. Now the company has refreshed its cute Stylophone Mini instrument for modern audiences.
The Mini was first introduced in 2010, but left production years ago. The new one is still extremely small, thus the name. A full-sized Stylophone can fit in a pants pocket, but the Mini is basically the size of a credit card. To that end, it includes a loop to connect it to a keychain or hang it from a car dashboard.
There doesn't look to be many changes here, but the refreshed Stylophone Mini is available in three colors. This includes pink, which is brand new.
However, I'm not sure what the company could've changed or added. This is an instrument that proudly wears its history on its sleeve, with little interest in modern accoutrements. The company's CEO said that "in the age of AI, we wanted to make something simple, fun and real." It looks like that mission has been accomplished.
Despite the diminutive size, this is still (more or less) a real-deal Stylophone. It has just as many keys as its larger sibling, comes with a stylus for playing and includes built-in speakers. It looks pretty nifty.
The best part? It's just $30. Stylophones have always been budget-friendly instruments and the technology here is about as simple as simple gets. The Mini is available right now.
Though Bowie was perhaps the most notable fan of the Stylophone, he wasn't the only big artist to find inspiration within its nickel-plated touch keyboard. Artists like The White Stripes, Kraftwerk, Blondie and Pulp have all used the device on records or during live performances. Even The Beatles fooled around with it while recording "Old Brown Shoe" during the Let it Be sessions, though it didn't make the final mix.

title_en: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro vs Amazon Fire HD 10: What's changed, and is the upgrade worth it?
title_fa: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro vs Amazon Fire HD 10: What's changed, and is the upgrade worth it?
excerpt_en: Amazon's best tablet ever didn't have to work hard for the title, but a new nanomatte screen and Kindle mode sweeten the deal.
excerpt_fa: Amazon's best tablet ever didn't have to work hard for the title, but a new nanomatte screen and Kindle mode sweeten the deal.
content_en:
Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro vs Amazon Fire HD 10: What's changed, and is the upgrade worth it?
Amazon's best tablet ever didn't have to work hard for the title, but a new nanomatte screen and Kindle mode sweeten the deal.
With a brand new series of tablets announced today, including the top-end Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro which usurps the Fire HD 10 at the top of the lineup, Amazon's hardware is better and bolder than before. That may sound like high praise, but the e-retailer's tablet lineup has always been aimed at the bargain bin rather than taking aim at the iPads and Galaxy Tabs of the world. This time around, the new hardware still doesn't reach those heights, but it flies cleanly in between and soars above its predecessor.
To hear Amazon tell it, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is built around two things that could hardly be further apart: reading, and lots of AI. To that end, its marquee features include a "nanomatte" display to better imitate paper, along with a new processor to power Alexa+, the AI-powered version of Amazon's long-running voice assistant. Whether or not you're enthused about the presence of AI here (Amazon would certainly like you to be), it's hard to turn down better hardware.
Compared to the Fire HD 10 tablet, which has until now occupied the top slot in Amazon's mobile hardware lineup since the Fire Max 11 was quietly discontinued in the US, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro appears to be a significant upgrade in all the ways that matter. Here's how Amazon is taking its new tablets up a notch.
Amazon's latest tablet is its best ever (but that's faint praise)
The previous flagship tablet in Amazon's lineup was the Fire HD 10, but to call it a flagship risks overstating its appeal. Its base model has just 32 gigabytes of storage and 4 gigabytes of RAM, which in combination with its practically ancient MediaTek Helios chip means it has roughly the performance of a cheap Chromebook. Slap a 10.1-inch WUXGA display on it, and you've got a device that's perfectly suited to watching videos or reading books, but which isn't a productivity machine. But at $155 for the base model, it's a clear bargain pick for those on short budgets or who don't need a lot of tablet to begin with.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is a massive upgrade in every regard. An aluminum build does away with the plastic elements of the Fire HD 10, and cradled inside is a 4-nanometer, 8-core MediaTek Dimensity 8400 CPU, which can be paired with up to 16 gigabytes of RAM. There are also two display options, a standard glossy display or a textured "nanomatte" one which should be better for reading. Both panels measure 12 inches with a pixel density of 280 pixels per-inch (with some quick math, roughly 2,880 by 1,920 is the closest standard resolution).
Software gets a big overhaul, too. Sure, there's a ton of Alexa+ integration — Amazon is the preeminent builder of data centers, after all — from the expected smart home controls to the ability to chat about what's on your screen or go hands-free in a live voice chat mode. But arguably the biggest change is the addition of the Google Play Store. We relayed last year that Amazon might be ditching its Fire OS software, and sure enough, we're seeing Android as the underlying software here. The new home screen seems to have ditched the storefront-like layout Fire tablet users are used to in favor of a more Alexa-focused experience.
Amazon goes back to its roots with a dedicated Kindle mode
One major reason to buy an Amazon tablet is as a Kindle alternative. If you read a lot of ebooks but want the ability to watch videos and run Android apps, Fire tablets have had your back. Of course, the Kindle app runs perfectly well on tablets from other brands, so Amazon is leaning hard into its first-party advantage with the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. In fact, all the new Alexa tablets announced today will offer a new Kindle mode, designed to "preserve the sanctuary of reading," according to Amazon's Panos Panay.
The updated Kindle reading experience will be enhanced if you're using the tablet with the optional nanomatte display. Amazon designed it in partnership with Corning, the company behind Gorilla Glass, to create a texture that lines up with the pixel grid in the panel. The upshot of this is that it should reduce screen glare, making it easier to read text in bright conditions. We've seen other new devices with similar finishes, including Apple's foldable iPhone Duo.
While reading in the Kindle app, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro will silence notifications, reduce blue light, and extend battery life (presumably by killing some background processes you don't need while stuck in the Kindle app). You can also pick from three display settings: warm, paper-like, or grayscale. We'll need to test this in order to know whether it's a better experience than, say, programming a Samsung tablet to enter do-not-disturb and turn on a blue light filter when you open the Kindle app. But if you're fully ensconced within the Kindle or Alexa ecosystems, this is one device to keep on your radar.
Pricing for the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the standard display version with 128GB of storage and 8GB of RAM, or $550 for the nanomatte display version with the same storage and memory configuration. There is also a Pro Keyboard case accessory for $150 and a Tablet Pro Pen stylus for $90, both sold separately.

title_en: The new BMW iX4 is the X4 reborn as an EV
title_fa: The new BMW iX4 is the X4 reborn as an EV
excerpt_en: BMW has brought the X4 design to its third Neue Klasse EV with an electric version called the iX4.
excerpt_fa: BMW has brought the X4 design to its third Neue Klasse EV with an electric version called the iX4.
content_en:
The new BMW iX4 is the X4 reborn as an EV
It offers a substantial 428 miles of EPA range and up to 603 horsepower.
You know a BMW X4 when you see one: it's a tall, compact SUV with a swooping rear roofline that looks both substantial and fast. Following the iX5, BMW has now brought that the X4's vibe to its third Neue Klasse EV with an electric version called the iX4. It carries the same form as the ICE model but adds the (in)famous Neue Klasse kidney grille, along with an electric drive train in two configurations offering substantial speed and range.
With short wheel overhangs and a sloping back, along with bulgy renders and an aggressive front grille design, the iX4 looks about as athletic as an SUV can be. Augmenting that is a substantial rear spoiler with an integrated brake light, along with low-profile rear taillights.
Both the iX4 50 xDrive and iX4 M60 xDrive offering impressive range, along with substantial power and torque (Europe has a third model, the iX4 40 xDrive). They come with a 112kWh battery good for up to an impressive 428 miles of EPA range on the 50 xDrive model, with the ability to charge from 10 to 80 percent in 21 minutes thanks to the 800-volt architecture. (The M60's range and charging specs have yet to be announced.)
The 50 xDrive's 463 horsepower and 475 pound-feet of torque can propel it from 0 to 60 mph in 4.7 seconds, with an electronically limited 130 mph top speed. The sportier iX4 M60 xDrive can hit that same 60 mph speed in 3.9 seconds, thanks to a bunch of extra horsepower and torque (603 hp and 465 pound-feet). It will also go faster on the Autobahn at 149 mph, again governed electronically.
The iX4 offers a suitably luxurious and high-tech interior as well, as we've seen in its other Neue Klasse vehicles. You get an optional 3D heads-up display, 17.9-inch center touchscreen and BMW's new vertical spoke steering wheel. The standard sound system is a seven spekaer, 205 watt setup, while M60 xDrive owners will get a 13-speaker, 430-watt Harman Kardon system as standard. The Panoramic iDrive assisted driving and infotainment systems are powered by BMW's Operating System X software (based on Android Open-Source Project).
The BMW iX4 50 xDrive will start at $67,695 when it arrives in showrooms on March 2027, about $10K less than the bigger iX5 60 eDrive EV. Pricing for the iX4 M60 xDrive has yet to be revealed, but it's likely to be around $20,000 more, based on BMW's typical M-vehicle surcharge.

The iX4 offers a suitably luxurious and high-tech interior as well, as we've seen in its other Neue Klasse vehicles. You get an optional 3D heads-up display, 17.9-inch center touchscreen and BMW's new vertical spoke steering wheel. The standard sound system is a seven spekaer, 205 watt setup, while M60 xDrive owners will get a 13-speaker, 430-watt Harman Kardon system as standard. The Panoramic iDrive assisted driving and infotainment systems are powered by BMW's Operating System X software (based on Android Open-Source Project).
The BMW iX4 50 xDrive will start at $67,695 when it arrives in showrooms on March 2027, about $10K less than the bigger iX5 60 eDrive EV. Pricing for the iX4 M60 xDrive has yet to be revealed, but it's likely to be around $20,000 more, based on BMW's typical M-vehicle surcharge.

title_en: GPT-6 is coming to all tiers of ChatGPT
title_fa: GPT-6 is coming to all tiers of ChatGPT
excerpt_en: OpenAI is rolling out GPT-6 to ChatGPT, and it will come with the capability to build more visual responses.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI is rolling out GPT-6 to ChatGPT, and it will come with the capability to build more visual responses.
content_en:
GPT-6 is coming to all tiers of ChatGPT
It will come with a capability called Intelligent UI.
OpenAI is rolling out GPT-6 to ChatGPT, and it will come with a capability called Intelligent UI that the company says allows it to return responses quickly with fully interactive user interfaces. The company trained GPT-6 to be better at everyday conversations and to compose more visual responses within the chatbot itself. Based on what you're asking, it could include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts and other interactive experiences in its replies.
If you ask it to help you plan for a dinner you're hosting, for instance, ChatGPT's response could include an interactive table with the amount of ingredients you have to buy based on the number of people you say are coming. It could also include checklists and follow-up forms you can answer to get more detailed help. But if pure text makes more sense, the model can decide not add any visuals. To shorten wait times for complex tasks, OpenAI gave the model the capability to answer while it's still thinking unlike other reasoning models that decide its output first. The company trained the model to compose responses across multiple messages, with each one adding useful information so that the final output is cohesive.
OpenAI says the interactive responses could help you understand complex topics more easily with visual aids. And, you can use the feature to create specialized tools for your needs, such as a calculator to help you decide on investments or on how to split a bill. Plus, you can also use it to recreate retro games within ChatGPT, like Snake. "Instead of fitting every question into the same conversational format, ChatGPT can combine UI, data, and actions to create entirely new ways for people to explore, understand, and interact with information," the company explained.
GPT‑6 with Intelligent UI has already started rolling out to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users around the world. It's powered by GPT-6 Sol if you're paying for those subscription tiers. If you have a Free or a low-cost Go account, you'll get access to the new model sometime today. It will be powered by GPT‑6 Luna, which isn't as capable as Sol, in those tiers.

title_en: India rejects Elon Musk’s claim of discrimination over Starlink launch
title_fa: India rejects Elon Musk’s claim of discrimination over Starlink launch
excerpt_en: Starlink is still awaiting security clearance before it can seek spectrum and begin commercial services in India.
excerpt_fa: Starlink is still awaiting security clearance before it can seek spectrum and begin commercial services in India.
content_en:
India has rejected Elon Musk’s claim that Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet service, is being unfairly blocked from launching in the country. The pushback comes as SpaceX struggles to turn years of regulatory work and partnerships with India’s biggest telecom operators into a commercial launch in one of the world’s largest internet markets.
On Wednesday, Musk accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s launch in India to maintain what he called their “monopolistic chokehold” on the country, without identifying them or providing evidence for his claim. He called the alleged blocking a “crime against the people of India” and argued that Starlink could bring affordable, high-speed internet to people who lack internet access.
Hours later, India’s Ministry of Communications pushed back, saying its regulatory framework for satellite communications is “fair and non-discriminatory.” The ministry said in a statement that Starlink and two other licensed satellite operators are all at “broadly the same regulatory stage.” It added that all three companies are undergoing security assessments that must be completed before they can seek spectrum, the radio frequencies that satellites use to send signal.
Starlink has spent over five years trying to enter India, a market with more than a billion internet subscribers. But it has yet to begin commercial services despite securing key regulatory approvals and partnering with telecom giants Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel last year. SpaceX has also set up a local team as it prepares for a launch, appointing former Payoneer executive Prabhakar Jayakumar to lead its India operations in December.
Musk’s comments came hours after Lauren Dreyer, Starlink’s vice president of business operations, appeared at a telecom industry conference, India Mobile Congress, in New Delhi and reiterated the company’s commitment to the market. “We stand ready to serve India,” Dreyer said, adding that Starlink wants to help realize Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of achieving universal connectivity across the country.
Starlink said it already has more than 20 gateway sites (the ground stations that link its satellites to the internet) and hundreds of antennas on the ground in India, and has adapted its operations to meet the country’s regulatory, security, and data-sovereignty requirements. Moreover, SpaceX has positioned its satellite network as a complement to — rather than a replacement for — India’s terrestrial telecom networks.
SpaceX first attempted to launch Starlink in India in 2021. The company, however, had to refund preorders for its equipment in early 2022 after the Indian government called it out for “booking/rendering the satellite internet service” before getting the necessary licenses.
Starlink has also previously clashed with India’s largest telecom operators over how satellite spectrum should be allocated. Starlink pushed for spectrum to be assigned administratively, while Reliance Jio argued that it should be auctioned — a position that could have made Starlink’s entry more expensive. India ultimately sided with Starlink’s preferred approach, deciding to allocate satellite spectrum administratively rather than through an auction.
Jio and Airtel, the two biggest Indian telcos, are also pursuing their own satellite internet services, even as they have agreed to distribute Starlink in India. Jio is working with satellite operator SES on satellite broadband, while Airtel is a major backer of Eutelsat OneWeb, another licensed satellite operator in India.
While the timing of Starlink’s India launch remains unclear, the company this week launched Starlink Mobile, which connects ordinary phones to satellites, in neighboring Bangladesh this week.
Starlink, India’s Ministry of Communications, Reliance Jio, and Bharti Airtel did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title_en: Robot data startup Mecka AI nabs $60M from Sequoia
title_fa: Robot data startup Mecka AI nabs $60M from Sequoia
excerpt_en: Mecka AI collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots. The startup pays people to record everyday tasks.
excerpt_fa: Mecka AI collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots. The startup pays people to record everyday tasks.
content_en:
Mecka AI, a startup that collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots, announced it has raised a $60 million Series B round led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Microsoft’s venture fund M12, and others. TechCrunch had previously reported that the startup was nearing a new funding round at a $500 million valuation.
Founded in 2024, the startup intends to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, and other data-labeling companies have done for LLMs. Those companies supply the human-generated data these systems learn from. Mecka pays people to record themselves doing everyday tasks, like making coffee or fixing cars, while wearing body sensors and using smartphones.
Other startups that collect real-world data for robot training include XDOF, which was in talks to raise a Series B round at a $1.2 billion valuation according to TechCrunch’s previous reporting. Human-data platforms that began with LLMs are also expanding into robotics, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

title_en: While VCs crowd into San Francisco, Endeavor Catalyst raises $320M for founders ‘elsewhere’
title_fa: While VCs crowd into San Francisco, Endeavor Catalyst raises $320M for founders ‘elsewhere’
excerpt_en: Endeavor Catalyst just raised $320 million to keep backing founders outside Silicon Valley. Half the profits go back to the nonprofit that finds them.
excerpt_fa: Endeavor Catalyst just raised $320 million to keep backing founders outside Silicon Valley. Half the profits go back to the nonprofit that finds them.
content_en:
Endeavor Catalyst has closed its fifth fund with $320 million in capital commitments, bringing the firm’s total assets under management to more than $850 million. The raise is good news for founders outside the Bay Area who risk getting overlooked as more funds focus squarely on AI companies in Silicon Valley.
Endeavor Catalyst is the venture arm of Endeavor, a New York-based global nonprofit that has spent 30 years supporting founders outside major tech hubs. (It calls all those other places “elsewhere” throughout its marketing materials.)
The fund is run by managing partner Allen Taylor, a 20-year veteran of the organization, and managing director Jackie Carmel, who joined Endeavor Catalyst 12 years ago, along with a 16-person team. The official general partner, though, is Endeavor itself. What that means, says Linda Rottenberg, who co-founded Endeavor and helped start Endeavor Catalyst in 2012, is that “half of the fund’s profits go back to Endeavor, so every investment helps the next generation of founders who are building elsewhere.”
The bar for those founders is pretty high. A person first has to get into Endeavor’s network, where he or she can access Endeavor’s mentoring and extensive network, and that’s hard. Last year, the group says it screened more than 10,000 candidates and picked 88. The network now has more than 3,100 entrepreneurs in over 50 countries.
When one of those founders’ companies raises at least $5 million in a round led by another institutional investor, Endeavor Catalyst can join in on the same terms as that lead. The team tells TechCrunch that checks usually run $1 million to $3 million but can’t exceed 10% of the round.
Over the next few years, they plan to make 40 to 50 investments annually, investing in up to 150 companies altogether with this new fund, they say.
Taylor, via an email exchange, wouldn’t share numbers on cash-on-cash returns tied to its earlier funds, but he did point to some impressive-sounding numbers. Across all five funds, he says, Endeavor Catalyst has backed 437 companies in 44 markets. Eighty-three of those startups are currently valued at $1 billion or more, he says, and the unit has seen 39 exits and 11 IPOs.
Some of the venture arm’s most valuable holdings right now include four-year-old ElevenLabs, the maker of AI voice tools that was recently valued at $22 billion in a secondary sale (it was founded in Poland originally), and Bending Spoons, the 13-year-old Italy-based conglomerate that went public in July and that currently boasts a $26 billion market cap.
Other holdings include New York-based Reflection AI (founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers — one of whom was born in Greece), which is now valued at $25 billion; Checkout.com, whose founder is Swiss and which was valued last year at $12 billion; the African payments infrastructure company Flutterwave, valued this summer at $3.2 billion; and AI coding startup Replit, co-founded by Amjad Masad, who is Palestinian-Jordanian. Replit snagged a $9 billion valuation earlier this year.
Endeavor, the nonprofit, has especially well-connected people associated with it, including board members Reid Hoffman; Nick Beim, a career VC who has spent the last 25 years at Matrix Partners, then Venrock; and Edgar Bronfman Jr., the former head of Warner Music and Seagram, who chairs Endeavor’s board.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis is a longtime friend of Endeavor, too, having gone to Harvard with Rottenberg. (Late last month in San Francisco, I sat down with him during a rare visit to the Bay Area that was organized by Endeavor and where he met with tech founders and Greek expatriates.)
Altogether, Endeavor Catalyst’s newest fund includes 400 limited partners, including Hoffman; famed hedge fund manager Bill Ackman; and the Dutch investment group Prosus. According to Taylor, roughly 30% of those backers are Endeavor founders themselves, including founders of Nubank, Revolut, and Checkout.com.
While so much attention is paid to what’s happening in San Francisco and its immediate environs right now, the bets of Endeavor Catalyst suggest what other investors may be missing, and Endeavor, with local teams and mentors in dozens of countries, seems particularly well-positioned to see it.
Indeed, about 90% of the venture arm’s investments are outside the U.S., it says. Europe is its fastest-growing region, with 12 new investments in the first half of 2026 compared with 14 in all of last year, though Latin America is still the largest.
Repeat founders are also becoming a bigger part of the mix. Taylor tells TechCrunch that roughly 14% of Endeavor Catalyst’s fourth fund went to second companies started by Endeavor founders at the seed or Series A stage. With this new fund, the team expects that number will reach 20%.
Pictured above: Endeavor co-founder Linda Rottenberg onstage in Turin, Italy, earlier this month.

title_en: Rivian R2 owners can now put a live pet cam on their phone's lockscreen
title_fa: Rivian R2 owners can now put a live pet cam on their phone's lockscreen
excerpt_en: Keep an eye on your furry, feathered or scaly friends when you leave the car.
excerpt_fa: Keep an eye on your furry, feathered or scaly friends when you leave the car.
content_en:
Rivian R2 owners can now put a live pet cam on their phone's lockscreen
Keep an eye on your furry, feathered or scaly friends when you leave the car.
Rivian's latest software update is one many pet parents will be very pleased to see. Following the latest 2026.36 update, R2 vehicle models will have the option to put a Pet Cam on your phone's lock screen in case you need to step away from the car while your critter is still inside. This feature leverages the high-definition interior camera in R2 models to show the vehicle's interior in the Rivian app. You'll be able to see a full livestream if you don't want to miss a minute of whatever your pet gets up to, or just see a regularly refreshed snapshot in the app dashboard or on your lock screen for a quick check. The Pet Cam can be stopped with a tap on the vehicle's main display.
The next software update also has further improvements coming to the Pet Mode that Rivian already made available for animal-friendly climate control when you're not on board. Now you can enable Pet Mode from the Rivian app, in case you forget to turn it on before leaving the vehicle. There will also be a confirmation prompt when toggling Pet Mode on or off from the app to avoid accidental changes that could put your canine companion, feline friend or awesome avian at risk. These controls will be available in all models from the company.
In non-pet news, R2 vehicles will also be seeing the debut of Rivian Assistant. The AI voice assistant is already available in R1 models, and it can be directed to handle simple tasks around navigation, entertainment and climate in the vehicle.

title_en: BMW’s iX4 SUV is a 428-mile defensive weapon against China’s EV takeover
title_fa: BMW’s iX4 SUV is a 428-mile defensive weapon against China’s EV takeover
excerpt_en: While much of the automotive world sits dumbfounded as China gobbles up all its customers, BMW continues to roll out extremely well-crafted, technologically advanced electric vehicles that impress in both drive quality and price. The latest is the BMW iX4, a coupe-shaped SUV...
excerpt_fa: While much of the automotive world sits dumbfounded as China gobbles up all its customers, BMW continues to roll out extremely well-crafted, technologically advanced electric vehicles that impress in both drive quality and price. The latest is the BMW iX4, a coupe-shaped SUV...
content_en:
While much of the automotive world sits dumbfounded as China gobbles up all its customers, BMW continues to roll out extremely well-crafted, technologically advanced electric vehicles that impress in both drive quality and price. The latest is the BMW iX4, a coupe-shaped SUV that puts a sportier spin on the automaker’s iX3.
BMW’s iX4 SUV is a 428-mile defensive weapon against China’s EV takeover
The iX4 is a sportier spin on the iX3, with the same powerful Gen6 battery providing class-leading range.
The iX4 is a sportier spin on the iX3, with the same powerful Gen6 battery providing class-leading range.
The iX4 is the third vehicle to be released on BMW’s next-generation Neue Klasse platform, following the iX3 and i3 models. The iX4 50 xDrive will come first in March 2027, followed by an even more high-performance M60 xDrive version later in the year. The automaker is positioning this new lineup as its bulwark against the flood of Chinese imports that is currently decimating other European brands. But while the iX4 can certainly compete on range and tech, it’s unclear whether BMW can rival China in terms of sheer affordability.
In that respect, the BMW iX4 50 xDrive starts at $66,200 (excluding fees for destination and handling). And it bears all the hallmarks of BMW’s other Neue Klasse models, such as the “Gen6” high-voltage battery with 112.2kWh of usable energy, an 800-volt architecture for lightning-quick charging top-ups, and up to 428 miles of range based on EPA estimates.
That’s more range than the Tesla Model Y, the best-selling electric vehicle in the world. BMW has been blowing away expectations on range to such a degree that even the experts at InsideEVs are left wondering whether it’s overkill. After all, Tesla and others have done plenty well with EVs in the mid-300s, while Lucid continues to struggle despite exceeding 500 miles in range.
But BMW wants to go the distance, believing that range and efficiency are two of its biggest selling points. The third would be performance, and thanks to a dual-motor setup in both the 50 xDrive and M60 xDrive, the iX4 is sure to delivery plenty of giddy up. The 50 xDrive’s motors put out 463 horsepower and 475lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60mph acceleration of 4.7 seconds. Meanwhile, the M60 xDrive’s motors produce 603hp and 645lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60 time a whole second less than the 50 xDrive.
Like other Neue Klasse vehicles, the electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) in the rear axle serves as the primary drive axle, using electricity instead of permanent magnets to power both its stator outer frame and interior spinning rotor. An inverter acts as the brain of the system, converting direct current from the battery into alternating current for the motor, regulating the electromagnets, and monitoring performance to keep the motor running as efficiently as possible. BMW says this combination helps slash drive-system energy losses by 40 percent and weight by 10 percent.
The Gen6 batteries are built with cylindrical lithium-ion cells measuring 46mm in diameter and 95mm in height that provide a 20 percent increase in energy density compared to the prismatic cells used in BMW’s Gen5 batteries. BMW has eliminated the traditional modules in favor of a “pack-to-open-body” construction where the battery housing serves as the vehicle’s underbody, lowering weight and increasing torsional rigidity.

With its 800V architecture, the iX4 can accept up to 400kWs of DC fast charging, replenishing up to 184 miles of range in 10 minutes, and 10–80 percent charge in just 21 minutes. title_en: The FCC proposes new mid-band spectrum auction and unlocking 800MHz for drones
title_fa: The FCC proposes new mid-band spectrum auction and unlocking 800MHz for drones
excerpt_en: The agency is doubling down on direct-to-device service.
excerpt_fa: The agency is doubling down on direct-to-device service.
content_en:
The FCC proposes new mid-band spectrum auction and unlocking 800MHz for drones
The agency is doubling down on direct-to-device service.
The US Federal Communications Commission laid out a trio of proposals for several rule changes around wireless connectivity. The plans will be put to a vote later this month and largely center on direct-to-device communications.
First, the agency suggested overhauling its rules for direct-to-device, or D2D, service. The stated goal is to "promote more flexible terrestrial, satellite, and hybrid business arrangements." Related, the second proposal is to auction 25 megahertz of mid-band spectrum. Bids would be targeting use cases such as "flexible-use terrestrial networks, innovative direct-to-device (D2D) operations, or a hybrid of both" according to the FCC. This could prove enticing to companies like Amazon, which are hoping to join the growing field of satellite-based cellular service.
One such company is SpaceX, which already has spectrum licenses it bought from EchoStar. Yesterday the FCC granted approval to SpaceX for a system of 15,000 satellites to operate at 330km. This push into D2D systems from SpaceX is a separate affair than the company's attempts to launch a network of orbital data centers aimed to provide compute power for artificial intelligence activity and would add to its existing network of more than 11,000 Starlink satellites. Suffice to say, SpaceX has a whole lot of gear overhead.
The final FCC proposal recommends allowing drones to operate on the 800MHz cellular band. Those devices are currently prohibited from using that frequency, and if passed, the change would open up about 50 megahertz for UAVs to use. Over the past year, the agency has been placing more restrictions on the drones that it deemed to be security risks, whether for containing foreign-made parts or for being equipped with tech such as LiDAR.

excerpt_fa: Teenage Engineering founder and CEO Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety that it plans to stop making synths. And yes, that includes the iconic OP-1, which put the company on the map. TE isn't just a music gear maker; it's also a sought-after design firm. It's collaborated with...
content_en:
Teenage Engineering founder and CEO Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety that it plans to stop making synths. And yes, that includes the iconic OP-1, which put the company on the map. TE isn’t just a music gear maker; it’s also a sought-after design firm. It’s collaborated with Ikea, Nothing, and Playdate, among others. But almost everything the company makes itself — the OP-1, the OP-XY, EP-133, TP-7, et cetera — is music or audio-focused. Which makes the supposed decision to abandon the market all the more confusing.
Teenage Engineering’s CEO says it’ll stop making synths
The end could be nigh for the iconic OP-1 according to a Highsnobiety interview.
The end could be nigh for the iconic OP-1 according to a Highsnobiety interview.
Here’s the relevant quote from Highsnobiety:
Kouthoofd tells me that, as part of a reorganization last fall, he announced to his team he is planning to stop making synthesizers altogether. The OP-1 is no exception. Launched in 2011, it put Teenage Engineering on the map and has been central to its success ever since.
“Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’ But I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business,” Kouthoofd says. “We can be so much more than that.”
Teenage Engineering did not immediately return a request for comment.

title_en: Nous Research confirms it hit $1.5B valuation, launches AI agents for business users
title_fa: Nous Research confirms it hit $1.5B valuation, launches AI agents for business users
excerpt_en: The developer of Hermes Agent raised a $90 million Series B.
excerpt_fa: The developer of Hermes Agent raised a $90 million Series B.
content_en:
Nous Research, the startup developing the open source Hermes Agent, has raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation, confirming TechCrunch’s earlier reporting.
The round was led by Robot Ventures, with participation from other backers including Nvidia, Union Square Ventures, Menlo Ventures, Samsung, and 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The new financing brings the three-year-old startup’s total funding to $158 million.
Popular among developers and individuals, the open source Hermes Agent has been cloned more than 24 million times, driving roughly 2.5% of global AI token usage, according to the startup’s estimates.
The capital will fund Nous Research’s push into the enterprise sector with “Hermes for Businesses,” allowing companies to deploy customized AI agents that can handle multi-step workflows while keeping their data private and secure.
Nous was at roughly $36 million in annualized revenue by mid-September 2026 and expects to pass $100 million before the end of 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported.

title_en: Android’s physical navigation buttons are back on Googlebooks, but not the way you think
title_fa: Android’s physical navigation buttons are back on Googlebooks, but not the way you think
excerpt_en: A common misconception I've seen with Googlebooks is that the Quick Insert and Google logo keys are new. They're not, as they first debuted a couple of years ago on some Chromebooks. But there is something new for Googlebooks that's ripped straight from Android phones circa...
excerpt_fa: A common misconception I've seen with Googlebooks is that the Quick Insert and Google logo keys are new. They're not, as they first debuted a couple of years ago on some Chromebooks. But there is something new for Googlebooks that's ripped straight from Android phones circa...
content_en:
A common misconception I’ve seen with Googlebooks is that the Quick Insert and Google logo keys are new. They’re not, as they first debuted a couple of years ago on some Chromebooks. But there is something new for Googlebooks that’s ripped straight from Android phones circa 2014.
Android’s physical navigation buttons are back on Googlebooks, but not the way you think
An oldie but a goodie — and kind of a necessity-die.
An oldie but a goodie — and kind of a necessity-die.
On every Googlebook keyboard, the F1, F2, and F3 keys are the old triangle, circle, and square navigation icons that first debuted on Android 5.0 Lollipop. These were the back, home, and app switcher buttons long before everything went to gesture-based navigation, and they’re still built into phones on Android 17 as an alternative. On Googlebook OS, these keys do what you expect: the left-pointing triangle goes back, the circle goes “home” by minimizing all open apps, and the square tiles your open apps like Mission Control on macOS / Task View on Windows.
It’s useful to have these buttons, and to have them matched across all Googlebooks. The back button seems sometimes necessary when using Android apps that aren’t really optimized for a desktop interface or mouse controls. I just wish a second press of the home button brought all your apps back to where they were, but that’s another feature called desktop peeking that uses a different keyboard shortcut.
If you’re an Android nerd of yore, it’s kind of fun to see these buttons live on. But they’re also a reminder that you sometimes need a fallback when Android gets all Android on you.

Just as we found a couple handfuls of goodies that are under $25, there are plenty of deals during Amazon’s October sale that are $50 or less, many of which offer a lot of practical value. Everything from chargers to coffee makers are discounted until 3 AM ET on October 8th, 2026, so you only have a few hours to take advantage of some of these deals.

This 412-piece set features the Mandalorian’s reconstructed Naboo starfighter, with minifigs for Din Djarin, Grogu, and Peli Motto.

EasySMX S10
The EasySMX S10 is our favorite Switch 2 controller for people who don’t want to spend twice as much on Nintendo’s option. It offers an excellent take on HD rumble, along with amiibo support and the ability to wake the Switch remotely.
Ridge Tracker Card
This incredibly slim tracking card is just 1.55 millimeters thick, compatible with both iOS and Android, and recharges wirelessly via MagSafe or Qi.

Hoto’s compact rechargeable electric screwdriver includes 12 magnetic tips. It’s great for quick fixes at home or on the go.

A smart plug adds functionality to an existing gadget rather than replacing it. Once the plug is connected to your Wi-Fi network and a gadget, you can turn it on and off using an app. TP-Link’s Tapo smart plug supports Matter, so you can add it to whichever smart home platform you use.
